opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the hardest problems right now. When I started in research, you could more or less read every relevant paper in your subfield. Today there are hundreds of papers a day on arXiv just in machine learning, and most of them, honestly, won't matter in two years. That's not a criticism; that's just how science works. But the volume makes the signal-to-noise problem much worse.

My own heuristic is to look for ideas that get *simpler* as they scale, not more complicated. A lot of papers propose a clever trick that gives you a point or two on a benchmark at a given scale, and then when you train a bigger model or use more data, the gain disappears. The bitter lesson, basically. The ideas that last tend to be the ones that let you use more compute or more data more effectively. Things like next-token prediction itself, instruction tuning, RLHF, using the model to generate its own training data. When we worked on Llama, a lot of the decisions came down to that question: does this still help when we scale up, or is it a crutch for a smaller regime?

The second thing I look at is whether an idea changes what people *do*, not just what they report. If practitioners quietly adopt something in their pipelines, even if the paper wasn't flashy, that's a strong signal. Conversely, a lot of papers get enormous attention on social media for a week and then nobody uses the method. So I try to wait a bit, see what survives contact with real training runs.

And the third is talking to people. Honestly, a lot of the filtering happens through conversations with researchers you trust, people who have actually tried things and can tell you, "Yeah, that doesn't replicate," or, "This one is real, we saw it too." That informal network is probably more valuable than any ranking or citation count right now, because citations lag so much behind the pace of the field.

So it's a mix: bias toward simplicity and scalability, watch for adoption rather than hype, and lean on people who get their hands dirty.

r001.rationale: The response says the volume worsens the signal-to-noise problem, but does not clearly say that valuable ideas may be overlooked.

r002.rationale: It contrasts today’s paper volume with an earlier time in the speaker’s career, but does not compare today’s problem with researchers’ problems roughly 30 years earlier or say today’s is preferable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, that's one of the questions I think about the most, because the volume right now is just insane. Thousands of papers a month, and if you tried to read even the abstracts you'd never do anything else.

So the first thing I'd say is that you have to accept you will miss things, and that's fine. The ideas that really matter tend to resurface. If something is truly important, you'll hear about it three, four times from different people, and that repetition is itself a signal. I don't try to be exhaustive anymore. I try to be well positioned so that good ideas find me, through people I trust, through what the team is actually running into when training models.

The second thing is that I've become a bit skeptical of benchmarks as the filter. A lot of papers are a small trick that gives you a point on some leaderboard, and most of those don't survive the next scale-up. What I look for instead is whether the idea tells me something about why things work. When we were doing Llama, the ideas that lasted were the simple ones that kept being true at every scale we tried. RLHF, synthetic data, scaling the right things. They were almost boring. The complicated architectural changes that looked clever at small scale mostly disappeared.

So my heuristic is something like: does this get simpler or more complicated as you add compute? If it gets simpler, if the trick becomes less necessary and the underlying principle becomes clearer, that's usually the sign of a lasting idea. If it needs more and more tuning to keep working, it's probably a patch on a problem that scale will solve anyway.

And the last thing, which sounds obvious but I think people underestimate, is that you have to actually try things. Reading a paper tells you very little. Running it on your own setup, at your own scale, with your own data, tells you a lot. Most of the signal I get doesn't come from reading, it comes from the gap between what a paper claims and what happens when we reproduce it. That gap is where you learn what's real.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the research volume is so high that one cannot read even the abstracts and must accept missing things, while discussing ideas that really matter.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare current research overload with challenges AI researchers faced roughly 30 years ago.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very hard to know in the moment. There are so many papers, and an improvement on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the underlying idea will matter in two years. I try to ask: what is the insight here? If you take away the particular model, the dataset, and the engineering details, is there something that changes how we should approach the problem?

Then you have to test it. Sometimes a very elegant idea doesn’t work, and sometimes a simple result points to something much deeper. So I think you need both curiosity and a willingness to be wrong. You develop intuitions about what matters, but you shouldn’t become too attached to them. The ideas that last tend to keep being useful as the models and the setting change.

r001.rationale: The response says the volume of papers makes it hard to tell which ideas will matter, but it does not say valuable ideas may be overlooked because of that volume.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare today’s research overload with the challenges AI researchers faced roughly 30 years ago.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very hard to know in the moment. There are so many papers, and something can look very exciting because it improves a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it changes how we think about the problem.

For me, the question is: what is the underlying idea, and why should it continue to work as we scale? If you remove the particular benchmark, the particular model, is there still something useful there? I tend to pay more attention to that than to the headline result.

And then you have to be willing to be wrong. You develop an intuition, you test it, and you update. Sometimes a simple idea that people overlook becomes very important once the rest of the technology catches up. Time is probably the best filter, but as a researcher, you still have to make bets before you have that clarity.

r001.rationale: The response mentions many papers and says simple ideas can be overlooked, but it does not connect the research volume to valuable ideas being overlooked.

r002.rationale: It does not compare today’s research overload with the problems AI researchers faced roughly 30 years ago.
